specAnchors.text: describe the stages in the carbon cycle, including respiration, photosynthesis, decomposition and combustion

primer.text: Carbon is the backbone of every living molecule, and the carbon cycle tracks where it travels. This note follows carbon from the air into plants by photosynthesis, along food chains through feeding, and back into the atmosphere through respiration, decomposition and combustion.

modules.title: Cycling Carbon Through Ecosystems
sourceHeadings: Uptake of carbon by living organisms
modules.opening: Carbon sits at the centre of every biological molecule, and plants constantly pull carbon dioxide out of the air to build the glucose that becomes their biomass, so the element keeps flowing through every ecosystem.
keyPoints: Carbon forms part of the biological molecules that build cells, such as carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Plants take carbon dioxide out of the air during photosynthesis.
The carbon captured becomes glucose, which plants turn into carbohydrates, fats and proteins in their biomass.

low.restatement: Green plants soak up carbon dioxide and lock the carbon into their own bodies.
low.analogy: A factory taking in raw material from the air and storing it as product stock.
low.examPointer: Quote photosynthesis as the uptake step and name glucose plus biomass as the products.

medium.restatement: Photosynthesis is the door through which carbon enters the living world: carbon dioxide goes in, glucose is assembled, and that glucose is rebuilt into the carbohydrates, fats and proteins that make up plant biomass.
medium.analogy: Plants are carbon importers — the atmosphere is the warehouse and their biomass is the shelf where the stock lands.
medium.examPointer: If asked where carbon enters the cycle, name photosynthesis and follow the carbon into glucose and then biomass.

modules.title: Putting Carbon Back into the Air
sourceHeadings: Transfer of carbon between living organisms
Release of carbon into the atmosphere
modules.opening: Feeding moves carbon from plants into animals and up the food chain, while respiration, decomposition and combustion each push carbon dioxide back into the air, closing the carbon loop.
keyPoints: Herbivores take in carbon when they feed on plants, and carnivores gain it by eating other animals.
Respiration in plants and animals releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead material and waste, releasing carbon dioxide.
Dead remains can become fossil fuels, and burning them by combustion returns carbon dioxide to the air.

low.restatement: Eating spreads carbon through the chain; breathing, rotting and burning send it home.
low.analogy: A relay race where the baton is handed on by feeders and thrown back by three different runners.
low.examPointer: Name all three release routes — respiration, decomposition and combustion — when tracing carbon back to the air.

medium.restatement: Carbon rides the food chain inside digested molecules, then leaves living bodies through respiration; decomposers finish off dead matter the same way, and any carbon buried into fossil fuels rejoins the atmosphere when combustion burns it.
medium.analogy: A library book passed reader to reader until it is finally returned to the shelf by three separate couriers.
medium.examPointer: Examiners want the full loop, so pair every transfer route with its release route in the same answer.

glossary.definition: The process in which plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air and build glucose inside their cells.
The living matter of an organism, built from carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
The process in living organisms that releases energy from food and returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
The breakdown of dead material and waste by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.
The burning of fuels such as fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide into the air.
